item.research_question: Can a quaternary tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) exhibit superior radiation resistance compared to pure tungsten, specifically regarding the formation of dislocation loops under fusion-relevant irradiation conditions?
item.material_system: Quaternary W-Ta-V-Cr high-entropy alloy with atomic composition 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V
item.processing_route: Magnetron sputtering deposition from pure metal targets (99.99% purity) using powers of 192 W (Cr), 312 W (V), 277 W (Ta), and 300 W (W) at 3 mtorr pressure and room temperature; films deposited on NaCl (100 nm) or Si (3 μm) substrates
item.test_conditions: In situ irradiation with 1-MeV Kr+2 at 1073 K up to 8 dpa (dose rate 0.0016 dpa s-1) and at room temperature up to 1.6 dpa; ex situ irradiation with 3-MeV Cu+ to ~17 dpa peak dose at 773 K and 1050 K; thermal annealing up to 1073 K; nanoindentation and TEM characterization
key_findings: The alloy exhibits a single-phase BCC structure with a bimodal grain size distribution: ~70% of grains are nanocrystalline (≤100 nm) and regions of ultrafine grains (100 to 500 nm).
No irradiation-created dislocation loops were observed in TEM images even after exposure to 8 dpa at 1073 K or 1.6 dpa at room temperature.
Black spots observed during irradiation were identified as Cr- and V-rich precipitates (~3 to 5 nm size, density ~0.03 nm-2) rather than dislocation loops via APT and two-beam TEM analysis.
APT analysis revealed strong segregation of Cr and V to grain boundaries and triple junctions, with precipitate composition of 62 at % Cr and 30 at % V.
The as-deposited film hardness was approximately 14 to 15 GPa, increasing slightly after thermal annealing and irradiation, indicating small irradiation hardening.
Thermal stability tests up to 1073 K showed no grain growth, though slight elemental segregation (black spots) appeared above 1023 K.
First-principles calculations predicted a strong thermodynamic driving force for Cr-V phase separation, consistent with experimental observations of precipitate formation.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the outstanding radiation resistance to the similar mobilities of vacancies and self-interstitials in the HEA, which maximizes defect recombination probability and minimizes defect clustering. This equal mobility is caused by the rough energy landscape induced by local lattice distortion and chemical disparity. Additionally, the high density of grain boundaries acts as preferential recombination sites, further reducing defect concentrations within the grains.
item.limitations: The study notes that performing defect identification procedures (like analyzing l and g vectors) is extremely challenging in nanocrystalline samples with small grains. The authors also mention that the slight compositional difference between experimental precipitates and simulation results might be a kinetic effect due to irradiation modifying the steady-state microstructure.
item.future_work: The authors state that the alloys are suitable for bulk production and ideal for applications requiring extreme irradiation conditions, implying future work should focus on scaling up production and testing in bulk forms for fusion structural applications.
quotes: The black spots observed in the irradiated HEA samples at high temperature are Cr- and V-rich precipitates and not irradiation-created dislocation loops.
Maximizing recombination will lead to a reduction in defect concentration and therefore a reduction in the kinetics of precipitation and growth of second-phase particles.
